`rcp`: copy files between computers.

## Synopsis

<strong>rcp</strong> \[<strong>-r</strong>\] <em>source</em> \[<em>source</em>...\] <em>target</em>

## Description

<strong>rcp</strong> copies files to or from another computer. The sources are all on one side and the target on the other: a remote name is <em>host</em><strong>:</strong><em>path</em> (<em>host</em> as <strong>rsh</strong>(1) takes it, found once for the whole copy); a name with no colon, or with a <strong>/</strong> before its colon, is local.

A target that's a directory (or ends with <strong>/</strong>) gets each source by its name in it; otherwise the source becomes the target. With more than one source, the target must be a directory.

It's <strong>rsh</strong> underneath, as BSD's rcp was: on the other computer, <strong>cat</strong> reads or writes each file, <strong>mkdir -p</strong> makes the directories, and <strong>find</strong> lists a remote directory's tree.

## Options

<strong>-r</strong>
: Copies directories, and everything in them. Without it, a directory source is refused. A link is copied as what it leads to (a file's contents); it's never followed into a directory.

## Exit status

0 when everything was copied; 1 when something couldn't be read or written (the rest is still copied), or the other computer can't be reached.

## Examples

```text
rcp /notes 1b9c0e:/notes
rcp 1b9c0e:/log /tmp/
rcp /a.lua /b.lua 1b9c0e:/bin/
rcp -r /projects 1b9c0e:/backup/
```

## Notes

BSD's rcp keeps files' times with <strong>-p</strong>; this one doesn't. Both ends being remote isn't supported.

## See also

<strong>rsh</strong>(1), <strong>cp</strong>(1)
